So basically, I have a huge amount of if/else processing to do, and I'm referencing arrays of objects so I have no choice but to use scripts to do so. The processing could be broken into several broad categories, and I'd rather make a separate common event to handle each broad category instead of making a single, massive, confusing (for me) if/else block handling each and every condition and sub-condition.
But unfortunately, I'm not seeing a way to call a common event through script that works the same way as when you use RPG Maker's (MZ) built-in command. I need the call to act like a subroutine, processing within the first script, then returning to that script and letting it continue from the jumping-off point.
As an alternative, I tried using the script for "jump to label." I checked the script call database, but I'm not understanding how to "set" the label (for MZ), only to jump to it. And I can't get it to jump to a label defined outside of the script. The instructions aren't as clear as they are for MV, or more likely my newb-brain just isn't getting it yet.
Anyway , I'd be fine if anyone could offer any solution that would work the way I've described. Thanks in advance.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
It seems (without seeing samples of your work) that what you're doing might benefit from outsourcing some of the script calls (or even events) to functions in a plugin file.
That way, you can call whatever you need and continue with the next event command.
Alternatively, you can de-modularize and instead of calling other events, just paste their commands into the appropriate places in your first event.

I think this question is different from what

The answer is that no, you don't need to do anything. All js files included in the project can use code from each other; you can just call functions and reference objects from the core files within your plugin. And
vice versa
between two plugins.
There's no #include or anything like that.
The answer above is giving a way to check whether a specific other plugin has been installed, but it's not necessary to reference its code.
